title: Rome and the rise of Christianity
note: Rome grew from a city-state into a republic that ruled the Mediterranean, then into an empire under Augustus. Christianity began in Roman Judea, spread along Roman roads, was persecuted, then legalized by Constantine in 313 CE and made the state religion by 380 CE.

read.title: From republic to Christian empire
text: After expelling its last king around 509 BCE, Rome governed itself as a republic. Two consuls, elected each year, led the state, and the Senate of aristocrats guided policy. Plebeians struggled for a larger voice and won their own officials, the tribunes, and written laws in the Twelve Tables. In three Punic Wars Rome defeated Carthage, and by 146 BCE no power in the Mediterranean could match it.

Conquest brought wealth but also unrest. Generals with loyal armies fought civil wars, and Julius Caesar made himself dictator before senators killed him in 44 BCE. His heir Octavian defeated his rivals and in 27 BCE took the name Augustus. He kept the forms of the Republic but ruled as the first emperor, opening the long Pax Romana.

In this peaceful, connected empire, Christianity spread from Judea to cities across the Mediterranean. Emperors at times persecuted Christians for refusing to honor the state gods. Then Constantine embraced the faith and, with the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, made it legal. In 380 CE Theodosius I declared Nicene Christianity the official religion. The western half of the empire weakened under pressure from Germanic peoples and ended in 476 CE, while the eastern half survived for nearly a thousand years.
